decks.title: Heights and Distances — Part 1: Angles of elevation and depression, one right triangle
goals: Draw a labelled figure and mark angles of elevation and depression
Read exact values and four-place table values
Find a height or a distance with one right triangle
Allow for eye height and state the precision

slides.heading: Heights and Distances, Part 1
slides.body_md: A tower, a rope or a roof: draw the right triangle, then use a ratio.

visual.alt: A tower FT 40 metres tall. An observer at P on the ground sees the top T at an angle of elevation of 30 degrees. From the top T a dashed horizontal line runs to the left, and the angle between it and the line of sight down to P is the angle of depression, also 30 degrees.
visual.caption: The angle of elevation at $P$ and the angle of depression at $T$ are both $30^\circ$.

slides.narration: Welcome to heights and distances. We find how tall a tower is, or how far away something is, without measuring it directly. We draw a right angled triangle, mark an angle of elevation or depression, and use one trigonometric ratio. In this part we use one triangle.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Draw a labelled figure and mark the **angle of elevation** or **depression**
Find a height or a distance from **one right triangle**
Allow for **eye height** and **round** as asked

nodes.label: Read the problem and draw a labelled figure
Mark the horizontal and the angle

visual.alt: Flow chart of the method: read the problem and draw a labelled figure, mark the horizontal and the angle, pick the right triangle, name the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, choose the ratio and solve, and answer with units and the stated precision.
visual.caption: Six steps for every heights-and-distances problem.

slides.narration: These are your goals. Draw a clear figure first. Mark the angle from the horizontal. Choose exact values or table values. Then solve one right triangle, remembering the height of the eyes, and round the answer as the question asks.

slides.heading: The angle of elevation
slides.body_md: The angle **above** the horizontal through the eye, up to the line of sight.

visual.alt: A column FT 30 metres tall on level ground. An observer at P on the ground looks up along the line of sight PT to the top T. The angle between the line of sight and the horizontal ground line PF is the angle of elevation, 35 degrees.
visual.caption: Angle of elevation: measured upward from the horizontal through the eye.

slides.narration: Stand at a point P on the ground and look up at the top of a column. The line of sight goes up. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal through your eye and that line of sight. It is always measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical.

slides.heading: The angle of depression
slides.body_md: The angle **below** the horizontal through the eye, down to the line of sight.

visual.alt: An observation deck T, 45 metres above the foot F, and a jogger at V on the ground. The dashed horizontal line from T and the line of sight TV make the angle of depression, 25 degrees, measured downward from the horizontal.
visual.caption: Angle of depression: measured downward from the horizontal through the eye.

slides.narration: Now stand on the top of a building and look down at a jogger. The line of sight goes down. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal through your eye and the line of sight to the jogger. Again the reference is the horizontal.

slides.heading: Depression equals elevation
slides.body_md: The horizontal through $T$ is parallel to the ground, so the two angles are **alternate angles**.

visual.alt: The same figure with two equal angles marked: the angle of depression of V from T is 25 degrees, and the angle of elevation of T from V is also 25 degrees, because the horizontal line through T is parallel to the ground FV and the angles are alternate.
visual.caption: Alternate angles: depression at $T$ = elevation at $V$.

slides.narration: The horizontal line through the observer on top is parallel to the ground. The line of sight is a transversal. So the angle of depression at the top equals the angle of elevation at the bottom. This lets us put the angle inside the right triangle, next to the ground.

slides.heading: Quick check: which line?
slides.body_md: Where is the angle of depression measured from?
slides.narration: Think about the horizontal line through the eye of the observer.

slides.heading: Exact values at standard angles
slides.body_md: At $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ keep **surds**, no decimals until the end.

visual.alt: Table of exact ratio values: at 30 degrees sine one half, cosine root three over two, tangent root three over three, cotangent root three; at 45 degrees sine and cosine root two over two, tangent and cotangent one; at 60 degrees sine root three over two, cosine one half, tangent root three, cotangent root three over three.
visual.caption: Exact values used when the angle is $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ or $60^\circ$.

slides.narration: For thirty, forty five and sixty degrees we use exact values. Tangent of thirty degrees is root three over three, tangent of forty five degrees is one, and tangent of sixty degrees is root three. Keep the roots in your working and convert to decimals only at the end.

slides.heading: Table values for other angles
slides.body_md: For other angles the question gives a table value, rounded to **four decimal places**.

visual.alt: Extract of trigonometric tables to four decimal places for 25, 35, 40 and 50 degrees: for example the tangent of 25 degrees is 0.4663, of 35 degrees 0.7002, of 40 degrees 0.8391 and of 50 degrees 1.1918.
visual.caption: Table values are rounded to four decimal places, so answers are approximate.

slides.narration: For other angles the question gives you values from the tables, to four decimal places. For example tangent of thirty five degrees is zero point seven zero zero two. Because the table values are rounded, an answer found with them is an approximation.

slides.heading: Which ratio?
slides.body_md: Name **opposite**, **adjacent** and **hypotenuse** for the marked angle first.

rows: angle and a slant length (rope, string, line of sight)

visual.alt: Table for choosing the ratio: height and ground distance give the angle with tangent; angle and ground distance give height as distance times tangent; angle and height give ground distance as height over tangent; angle and a slant length give height with sine and ground distance with cosine.
visual.caption: Name the sides first, then choose the ratio that links the two you use.

slides.narration: Always name the sides first. If you know the height and the ground distance, use tangent. A rope, a string or a line of sight is the hypotenuse, so use sine to find the height and cosine to find the ground distance. Choose the ratio that links the two sides in play.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a kite on a string
slides.body_md: A kite string $80$ m long, pulled taut, makes $30^\circ$ with level ground. Find the height of the kite.
bullets: **Step 1 —** The string is the hypotenuse and $h$ is opposite $30^\circ$: use sine.
**Answer —** $h = 40$ m. The horizontal reach is $40\sqrt{3} = 69.3$ m.

visual.alt: A kite K flying on a taut string OK of length 80 metres held at O. The string makes an angle of 30 degrees with the level ground. F is the point of the ground directly below the kite, and KF is the height h of the kite.
visual.caption: The string is the hypotenuse; the height $h$ is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle.

slides.narration: The string is the hypotenuse and the height is opposite the thirty degree angle, so use sine. Eighty times one half is forty. The kite is forty metres high. The horizontal distance is eighty cosine thirty degrees, forty root three, about sixty nine point three metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a pole from the tables
slides.body_md: Use $\tan 36^\circ = 0.7265$ and round to $0.1$ m.
slides.narration: Name the sides. The distance is adjacent and the height is opposite, so multiply the distance by the tangent from the table.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a tower with tables
slides.body_md: A point $P$ is $48$ m from the foot of a water-tank tower. The angle of elevation of the top is $52^\circ$. Using $\tan 52^\circ = 1.2799$, find the height to the nearest $0.1$ m.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $h$ is opposite $52^\circ$ and $48$ m is adjacent: tangent.

visual.alt: A water-tank tower FT of unknown height h. A point P on level ground is 48 metres from the foot F, and the angle of elevation of the top T from P is 52 degrees.
visual.caption: Known: $PF = 48$ m and the angle $52^\circ$; unknown: $h = FT$.

slides.narration: The height is opposite the fifty two degree angle and forty eight metres is adjacent, so use tangent. Height equals forty eight times one point two seven nine nine, which is sixty one point four three. To the nearest tenth of a metre the tower is sixty one point four metres tall.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: looking down
slides.body_md: From a rooftop restaurant $72$ m above the ground, a jetty is seen at an angle of depression of $25^\circ$. Using $\tan 25^\circ = 0.4663$, find its horizontal distance from the building.
bullets: **Step 1 —** The angle at the jetty is also $25^\circ$ (alternate angles).

visual.alt: A rooftop restaurant T, 72 metres above the foot F of the building. A boat jetty V on the level ground is seen from T at an angle of depression of 25 degrees. The distance d from F to V is to be found.
visual.caption: The depression $25^\circ$ at $T$ gives the angle $25^\circ$ at $V$.

slides.narration: By alternate angles the angle at the jetty is twenty five degrees. The height seventy two is opposite and the distance d is adjacent. Tangent twenty five degrees equals seventy two over d, so d is seventy two divided by zero point four six six three, one hundred fifty four point four metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a window and a bin
slides.body_md: The angle of depression is $45^\circ$ and the window is $12$ m up.
slides.narration: The tangent of forty five degrees is one, so the distance equals the height.

slides.heading: Eye height
slides.body_md: The angle is measured at the **eye**, so the figure has two levels.

visual.alt: A surveyor whose eyes E are 1.6 metres above the ground at P looks at the top T of a mast 30 metres away. The dashed horizontal line through E meets the mast at H. The angle of elevation of T from E is 40 degrees, so the part HT above eye level is found first, and the eye height is added at the end.
visual.caption: The angle is measured at the eye $E$, so $HT$ is the height above eye level.

slides.narration: When a person measures an angle, it is measured at the eyes, not at the ground. The horizontal line through the eyes meets the tower at H. The right triangle gives the height above eye level, H to T. The height of the eyes must be added at the end.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: adding the eye height
slides.body_md: A surveyor whose eyes are $1.6$ m above the ground stands $30$ m from a mast and sees its top at $40^\circ$. Use $\tan 40^\circ = 0.8391$ and find the height of the mast to $0.1$ m.

visual.alt: Working table for the surveyor: the part of the mast above eye level is thirty times tangent forty degrees, which is twenty-five point one seven three metres; adding the eye height of one point six metres gives twenty-six point seven seven three, so the mast is twenty-six point eight metres tall.
visual.caption: The angle belongs to the eye, so the eye height is added at the end.

slides.narration: First find the part of the mast above the surveyor eye level. It is thirty times tangent forty degrees, twenty five point one seven three metres. Then add the height of the eyes, one point six metres, to get twenty six point seven seven three. To the nearest tenth, the mast is twenty six point eight metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: Which line is the reference for both angles?
slides.narration: Recall where each angle is measured from.

slides.heading: Precision and rounding
slides.body_md: Table values and exact values agree after rounding. **Round once, at the end**, and state the precision.

visual.alt: Table showing that the exact value and the value from four-place tables agree after rounding to the nearest 0.1 metre: forty-eight tangent fifty-two degrees is sixty-one point four, seventy-two over tangent twenty-five degrees is one hundred fifty-four point four, and sixty-five tangent thirty-eight degrees is fifty point eight.
visual.caption: Round only at the end, and state the precision.

slides.narration: Here the exact value and the value from four place tables are compared. They differ only in the fourth decimal place, so after rounding to the nearest tenth of a metre they give the same answer. Keep extra digits in the working and round only the final answer.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal; depression at the top equals elevation at the bottom
Name the sides, then choose tangent, sine or cosine
Add the eye height; round at the end

rows: both measured from the horizontal through the eye; depression at the top $=$ elevation at the bottom
height and ground distance: tangent; slant length: sine or cosine
use surds at $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$; tables to four places otherwise
add it to the height found above eye level
round at the end and state it: nearest $0.1$ m

visual.alt: Summary table for part one: elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal; choose tangent, sine or cosine from the sides named; use exact values at standard angles and tables otherwise; add the eye height; and round at the end.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Both angles are measured from the horizontal. Name the sides and pick the ratio. Use exact values at the standard angles and tables for others. Add the height of the eyes when the observer is not at ground level, and round at the end as the question asks.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **One-triangle problem (3 marks):** figure or angle identified 1 + ratio equation 1 + answer with units 1
**Always draw** a labelled figure and mark the angle from the horizontal
**State the precision** you used, such as the nearest $0.1$ m
**Mistake:** dividing where you should multiply, or the reverse
slides.narration: In the exam, draw the figure. It usually earns a mark by itself. Write the ratio equation, solve, and give the answer with units and the precision asked for. Check whether you should multiply or divide, and never forget the eye height when it is given.

decks.title: Heights and Distances — Part 2: Problems with two right-angled triangles
goals: Link two triangles through a shared height
Find the height of an object on top of another
Check a two-triangle answer before finishing

slides.heading: Heights and Distances, Part 2
slides.body_md: Two angles, one height: the shared side joins two right triangles.

nodes.label: Write each distance from the foot as $h\cot\theta$
Same side: the distances differ by the gap
Opposite sides: the distances add to the gap

visual.alt: Flow chart for two triangles: both triangles share the height h; write each ground distance from the foot as h times cotangent of its angle; on the same side the distances differ by the gap, on opposite sides they add to the gap; then solve the single equation for h.
visual.caption: The common height links the two triangles.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Many problems give two angles, from two places, or to two points. Then there are two right angled triangles. They always share a side, the height or the distance from the foot, and that shared side lets us write one equation.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Join two triangles through the **shared height**
Find the height of an **object on top**
Run a **final check** on the answer

rows: Is every angle measured from the horizontal?
a vertical reference gives the complementary angle
Do both triangles use the same height or the same base?
that shared side links the two equations
subtract the distances for the same side, add for opposite sides
the angle is measured at the eye
Does the answer look sensible, with units and precision stated?
a taller object from a nearer point means a larger angle

visual.alt: Checklist for two-triangle problems: measure every angle from the horizontal; find the shared height or base; decide same side or opposite sides; include the eye height; and test that the answer is sensible with units and precision.
visual.caption: Five checks that catch most lost marks.

slides.narration: These are your goals. Join two triangles through the shared side. Decide whether the two points are on the same side or opposite sides. Handle an object standing on top of another. And finish with a quick check that catches most lost marks.

slides.heading: Two triangles, one height
slides.body_md: Both points look at the same top $T$, so $FT = h$ in both triangles.

visual.alt: A tower FT of height h with two points P and Q on level ground in line with its foot F on the same side. Q is nearer. From P the top T is seen at an angle of elevation of 30 degrees and from Q at 45 degrees. P and Q are 24 metres apart.
visual.caption: Two right triangles $PFT$ and $QFT$ share the height $FT = h$.

slides.narration: Here two points P and Q lie in line with the foot of the tower on the same side. From P the elevation is thirty degrees, from Q forty five degrees. Both triangles contain the same height. The ground distances are h cotangent of each angle, and they differ by twenty four metres.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: same side
slides.body_md: The top of a tower is seen at $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ from two points $24$ m apart, in line with its foot and on the same side. Find the height of the tower.

visual.alt: Working table: let the nearer distance be x; the height equals x times tangent forty-five degrees, which is x; the height also equals x plus twenty-four, over root three; equating gives root three x equals x plus twenty-four, so x is twelve times root three plus one; the height is thirty-two point eight metres.
visual.caption: Same side: the far distance exceeds the near one by the gap.

slides.narration: Let the nearer distance be x. From the nearer point the height equals x, because tangent forty five degrees is one. From the farther point the height is x plus twenty four over root three. Equate: root three x equals x plus twenty four. So x is twelve times root three plus one, and the height is thirty two point eight metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: the equation
slides.body_md: Which equation links the two triangles?
slides.narration: Both triangles share the height. Write the height from each point and equate.

slides.heading: Points on opposite sides
slides.body_md: From the top, depressions to **two sides**: each distance is $h\cot\theta$ and the distances **add**.

visual.alt: A sky-walk D, 48 metres above the point F on level ground, with two points A and B on opposite sides of F. From D the angle of depression of A on the left is 60 degrees and of B on the right is 45 degrees. Dashed horizontal lines through D show where the angles are measured from.
visual.caption: Opposite sides: the two distances add, $AB = AF + FB$.

slides.narration: Now the two points are on opposite sides of the foot. From the sky walk D, the left point is seen at sixty degrees depression and the right point at forty five degrees. By alternate angles these equal the angles of elevation at the points. The two distances from the foot add to give the gap.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: opposite sides
slides.body_md: A sky-walk is $48$ m above level ground. Two points on opposite sides of the point below it are seen at depressions of $60^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. Find the distance between the points.

rows: at $A$ the elevation is $60^\circ$; at $B$ it is $45^\circ$

visual.alt: Working table: by alternate angles the elevations at the two points are sixty and forty-five degrees; the left point is forty-eight cotangent sixty degrees, which is sixteen root three, from the foot; the right point is forty-eight metres away; on opposite sides the distances add, giving seventy-five point seven metres.
visual.caption: Opposite sides: add the two distances.

slides.narration: By alternate angles the elevations at the two points are sixty and forty five degrees. The left point is forty eight cotangent sixty degrees, sixteen root three metres, from the foot. The right point is forty eight metres from the foot. They are on opposite sides, so we add. The distance is seventy five point seven metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: the ratio of distances
slides.body_md: Test the statement with cotangents.
slides.narration: Write the distance from the foot for each angle as the height times the cotangent, and compare the two.

slides.heading: An object on top of another
slides.body_md: A finial, flagstaff or statue: subtract the **height of the bottom** from the **height of the top**.

visual.alt: A temple tower with a finial BT on top. From a point P on level ground 36 metres from the foot F of the tower, the angle of elevation of the bottom B of the finial is 45 degrees and of its top T is 52 degrees. The finial length f is the difference of the two heights.
visual.caption: Finial $f = FT - FB$, with both heights read from the same base $PF$.

slides.narration: Sometimes an object stands on top of a tower. From one point we see the bottom of the object at one angle and its top at a larger angle. Both heights are read from the same ground distance, so the length of the object is the difference of the two heights.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a finial
slides.body_md: From a point $36$ m from the foot of a temple tower, the angles of elevation of the bottom and top of its finial are $45^\circ$ and $52^\circ$. Using $\tan 52^\circ = 1.2799$, find the length of the finial.

visual.alt: Working table for the finial: the bottom is thirty-six metres high since tangent forty-five degrees is one; the top is thirty-six times one point two seven nine nine, which is forty-six point zero eight metres; the finial is the difference, ten point one metres.
visual.caption: Subtract two heights read from the same base.

slides.narration: The bottom of the finial is thirty six metres high because tangent forty five degrees is one. The top is thirty six times one point two seven nine nine, forty six point zero eight metres. The finial is the difference, ten point one metres to the nearest tenth.

slides.heading: Quick check: a pole and a tower
slides.body_md: Find the distance first, then the drop.
slides.narration: The distance to the foot is common to both depression triangles.

slides.heading: A walker or a vehicle approaching
slides.body_md: Moving towards the tower: the **gap walked** is the difference of the two distances from the foot.

visual.alt: A tower FT seen by a walker, first from A at an angle of elevation of 36 degrees and then from B, 24 metres closer on the same straight path to the foot F, at 52 degrees.
visual.caption: A walker moves $24$ m towards the tower: the elevation rises from $36^\circ$ to $52^\circ$.

slides.narration: A walker moves twenty four metres towards a tower. At the first point the elevation is thirty six degrees, at the second fifty two degrees. The twenty four metres is not the distance to the foot. It is the difference between the two distances, so we again use the height in both triangles.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the walker
slides.body_md: A walker moves $24$ m towards a tower; the elevation changes from $36^\circ$ to $52^\circ$. Using $\cot 36^\circ = 1.3764$ and $\cot 52^\circ = 0.7813$, find the height and the final distance from the foot.

visual.alt: Working table for the walker: the distances from the foot are h cotangent thirty-six degrees and h cotangent fifty-two degrees; they differ by twenty-four, so h times zero point five nine five one equals twenty-four, giving a height of forty point three metres; the second point is thirty-one point five metres from the foot.
visual.caption: Cotangent turns each angle into a distance from the foot.

slides.narration: Write each distance from the foot as the height times a cotangent. Their difference is twenty four. So h times zero point five nine five one equals twenty four, and h is forty point three metres. The final distance from the foot is forty point three times zero point seven eight one three, thirty one point five metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a boat approaches
slides.body_md: Explain why the angle grows as the boat gets closer.
slides.narration: Recall that tangent of the angle is height divided by distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a building and a tower
slides.body_md: From the top of an $18$ m building, the foot of a tower is seen at a depression of $60^\circ$ and its top at an elevation of $30^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.

visual.alt: An 18 metre building AG and a tower FT on the same level ground. From the top A of the building, the foot F of the tower is seen at an angle of depression of 60 degrees and the top T at an angle of elevation of 30 degrees. The dashed line AX is horizontal.
visual.caption: Depression $60^\circ$ to the foot, elevation $30^\circ$ to the top: two triangles at $A$.

slides.narration: By alternate angles the foot of the tower is eighteen cotangent sixty degrees, six root three metres, from the building. In the upper triangle the part of the tower above the roof is six root three times tangent thirty degrees, which is six metres. The tower is eighteen plus six, twenty four metres tall.

slides.heading: Angles do not scale
slides.body_md: Never use proportion on angles: use the **tangent ratio**.

headers: Distance of observer from a $30$ m tower

visual.alt: Table showing that a 30 metre tower seen from 30 metres has an elevation of 45 degrees, from 60 metres 26.6 degrees and from 120 metres 14.0 degrees: doubling the distance does not halve the angle.
visual.caption: Doubling the distance does not halve the angle: use the ratio, not proportion.

slides.narration: A common mistake is to think that doubling the distance halves the angle. It does not. A thirty metre tower is seen at forty five degrees from thirty metres, but only about twenty six point six degrees from sixty metres. The ratio is what scales, not the angle.

slides.heading: Five checks before you finish
slides.body_md: A short routine for every two-triangle problem.

rows: Is every angle measured from the horizontal?
a vertical reference gives the complementary angle
Do both triangles use the same height or the same base?
that shared side links the two equations
subtract the distances for the same side, add for opposite sides
the angle is measured at the eye
Does the answer look sensible, with units and precision stated?
a taller object from a nearer point means a larger angle

visual.alt: Checklist for two-triangle problems: measure every angle from the horizontal; find the shared height or base; decide same side or opposite sides; include the eye height; and test that the answer is sensible with units and precision.
visual.caption: Five checks that catch most lost marks.

slides.narration: Before you finish, run these five checks. Is each angle measured from the horizontal? Do both triangles share a height or distance? Same side or opposite sides? Is the eye height included? And is the answer sensible, with units and the precision stated?

slides.heading: Common slips
slides.body_md: These cost marks most often.

rows: measure from the horizontal through the eye
Multiplying where the height must be divided
unknown distance: height divided by tangent
Treating the walked distance as the distance to the foot
use two triangles: the gap is the difference
same side: subtract; opposite sides: add
keep surds or four places; round at the end

visual.alt: Table of common slips and fixes: measure depression from the horizontal; divide the height by tangent to find a distance; treat the walked distance as a gap between two distances; subtract for the same side and add for opposite sides; and round only at the end.
visual.caption: Four slips that cost the most marks.

slides.narration: Watch these slips. Do not measure a depression from the vertical. Divide the height by tangent to get a distance. Do not treat the walked distance as the distance to the foot. Subtract for the same side, add for opposite sides, and round only at the end.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Two triangles share a **height** or a **distance from the foot**
Same side: subtract; opposite sides: add
Object on top: subtract the heights
At most **two** right-angled triangles in one vertical plane

rows: both triangles share the height $h$ (or the distance from the foot)
subtract the heights to the bottom and the top
at most two right-angled triangles, in one vertical plane

visual.alt: Summary table for part two: both triangles share the height; on the same side the cotangent terms subtract to the gap; on opposite sides they add; for an object on top subtract the two heights; at most two right triangles in one plane.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Two triangles share a side, and that gives one equation. On the same side the cotangent terms subtract to the gap, on opposite sides they add. An object on top is a difference of heights. Problems at this level use at most two right angled triangles in one plane.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Two-triangle problem (4 marks):** figure 1 + first triangle 1 + second triangle or equation 1 + answer 1
**Name the shared side** in your working
**Use exact values** when the angles are $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$
**Mistake:** adding distances for points on the same side
**Mistake:** treating the walked distance as the distance to the foot
slides.narration: Examiners reward the figure, the first triangle, the equation linking the second, and the answer with units. Name the shared side. Use exact values at the standard angles and tables for the rest. And remember: subtract for the same side, add for opposite sides.

notes.title: Heights and Distances — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Angles of elevation and depression
sections.body_md:
The **angle of elevation** is the angle between the horizontal through the observer's eye and the line of sight to an object **above** eye level. The **angle of depression** is the angle between that horizontal and the line of sight to an object **below** eye level. Both are measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical.

Because the horizontal through the observer is parallel to the ground, the angle of depression of an object equals the angle of elevation of the observer (alternate angles).

*Example:* from a $45$ m deck a jogger is seen at a depression of $25^\circ$, so the angle at the jogger is $25^\circ$ inside the right triangle.

key_terms.definition_md: Angle above the horizontal through the eye, up to the line of sight.
Angle below the horizontal through the eye, down to the line of sight.
The straight line from the eye to the object looked at.

visual.alt: A tower FT 40 metres tall. An observer at P on the ground sees the top T at an angle of elevation of 30 degrees. From the top T a dashed horizontal line runs to the left, and the angle between it and the line of sight down to P is the angle of depression, also 30 degrees.
visual.caption: The angle of elevation at $P$ and the angle of depression at $T$ are both $30^\circ$.

visuals.alt: The same figure with two equal angles marked: the angle of depression of V from T is 25 degrees, and the angle of elevation of T from V is also 25 degrees, because the horizontal line through T is parallel to the ground FV and the angles are alternate.
visuals.caption: Alternate angles: depression at $T$ = elevation at $V$.

sections.heading: 2. Exact values and the trigonometric tables
sections.body_md:
At $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ use exact values: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$, and the sines and cosines from the table. For other angles, read the value from the tables, which are rounded to **four decimal places**, for example $\tan 35^\circ = 0.7002$.

An answer found with table values is approximate. Say how you rounded: "correct to the nearest $0.1$ m".

*Example:* with $\tan 40^\circ = 0.8391$, $18\tan 40^\circ = 15.1$ m.

key_terms.definition_md: A ratio read from the tables, rounded to four decimal places.

visual.alt: Table of exact ratio values: at 30 degrees sine one half, cosine root three over two, tangent root three over three, cotangent root three; at 45 degrees sine and cosine root two over two, tangent and cotangent one; at 60 degrees sine root three over two, cosine one half, tangent root three, cotangent root three over three.
visual.caption: Exact values used when the angle is $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ or $60^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Extract of trigonometric tables to four decimal places for 25, 35, 40 and 50 degrees: for example the tangent of 25 degrees is 0.4663, of 35 degrees 0.7002, of 40 degrees 0.8391 and of 50 degrees 1.1918.
visuals.caption: Table values are rounded to four decimal places, so answers are approximate.

sections.heading: 3. One right triangle: choosing the ratio

key_terms.definition_md: The side opposite the right angle: the rope, string or line of sight.

rows: angle and a slant length (rope, string, line of sight)

visual.alt: Table for choosing the ratio: height and ground distance give the angle with tangent; angle and ground distance give height as distance times tangent; angle and height give ground distance as height over tangent; angle and a slant length give height with sine and ground distance with cosine.
visual.caption: Name the sides first, then choose the ratio that links the two you use.

visuals.alt: A kite K flying on a taut string OK of length 80 metres held at O. The string makes an angle of 30 degrees with the level ground. F is the point of the ground directly below the kite, and KF is the height h of the kite.
visuals.caption: The string is the hypotenuse; the height $h$ is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle.

rows: $80$ m is the hypotenuse; $h$ is opposite $30^\circ$

visuals.alt: Working table for the kite: the string of eighty metres is the hypotenuse and the height is opposite thirty degrees, so use sine; height eighty times one half is forty metres; horizontal reach is forty root three, which is sixty-nine point three metres.
visuals.caption: Slant length and angle: sine for height, cosine for reach.

visuals.alt: A water-tank tower FT of unknown height h. A point P on level ground is 48 metres from the foot F, and the angle of elevation of the top T from P is 52 degrees.
visuals.caption: Known: $PF = 48$ m and the angle $52^\circ$; unknown: $h = FT$.

visuals.alt: Working table for the water-tank tower: height is opposite fifty-two degrees and forty-eight metres is adjacent, so use tangent; height equals forty-eight times tangent fifty-two degrees; the table gives one point two seven nine nine, and forty-eight times that is sixty-one point four three, which is sixty-one point four metres.
visuals.caption: Opposite and adjacent: tangent.

visuals.alt: A rooftop restaurant T, 72 metres above the foot F of the building. A boat jetty V on the level ground is seen from T at an angle of depression of 25 degrees. The distance d from F to V is to be found.
visuals.caption: The depression $25^\circ$ at $T$ gives the angle $25^\circ$ at $V$.

rows: the height is divided, not multiplied

visuals.alt: Working table for the boat jetty: by alternate angles the angle at V is twenty-five degrees; tangent of twenty-five degrees equals seventy-two over d, so d is seventy-two divided by zero point four six six three, which is one hundred fifty-four point four metres.
visuals.caption: When the height is known and the distance is wanted, divide by the tangent.

sections.heading: 4. Eye height and precision
sections.body_md:
The angle is measured at the observer's **eye**. If the eye is $e$ m above the ground, the right triangle gives the height above eye level, and

$$\text{height of the object} = e + \text{distance}\times\tan\theta.$$

Keep surds or extra decimals in the working, and **round once, at the end**, to the precision asked. A table-based answer and an exact answer agree after rounding.

*Example:* $e = 1.6$ m, distance $30$ m, $\theta = 40^\circ$: $1.6 + 30\times 0.8391 = 26.8$ m.

key_terms.definition_md: The height of the observer's eyes above the ground, added to the height above eye level.

visual.alt: A surveyor whose eyes E are 1.6 metres above the ground at P looks at the top T of a mast 30 metres away. The dashed horizontal line through E meets the mast at H. The angle of elevation of T from E is 40 degrees, so the part HT above eye level is found first, and the eye height is added at the end.
visual.caption: The angle is measured at the eye $E$, so $HT$ is the height above eye level.

visuals.alt: Working table for the surveyor: the part of the mast above eye level is thirty times tangent forty degrees, which is twenty-five point one seven three metres; adding the eye height of one point six metres gives twenty-six point seven seven three, so the mast is twenty-six point eight metres tall.
visuals.caption: The angle belongs to the eye, so the eye height is added at the end.

visuals.alt: Table showing that the exact value and the value from four-place tables agree after rounding to the nearest 0.1 metre: forty-eight tangent fifty-two degrees is sixty-one point four, seventy-two over tangent twenty-five degrees is one hundred fifty-four point four, and sixty-five tangent thirty-eight degrees is fifty point eight.
visuals.caption: Round only at the end, and state the precision.

sections.heading: 5. Two triangles: points on the same side
sections.body_md:
Two points $P$ and $Q$ in line with the foot $F$ of a tower, on the same side, give two right triangles with the **same height** $h$. With $QF$ nearer, elevations $\alpha$ at $P$ and $\beta$ at $Q$, and $PQ = d$:

$$h\cot\alpha - h\cot\beta = d, \qquad h = \dfrac{d}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}.$$

*Example:* $d = 24$, $\alpha = 30^\circ$, $\beta = 45^\circ$ gives $h = 12(\sqrt{3} + 1) = 32.8$ m. A walker who moves $24$ m towards the tower is the same problem: $24$ m is a **gap**, not the distance to the foot.

key_terms.definition_md: The height (or the distance from the foot) common to both right triangles.

visual.alt: A tower FT of height h with two points P and Q on level ground in line with its foot F on the same side. Q is nearer. From P the top T is seen at an angle of elevation of 30 degrees and from Q at 45 degrees. P and Q are 24 metres apart.
visual.caption: Two right triangles $PFT$ and $QFT$ share the height $FT = h$.

visuals.alt: Working table: let the nearer distance be x; the height equals x times tangent forty-five degrees, which is x; the height also equals x plus twenty-four, over root three; equating gives root three x equals x plus twenty-four, so x is twelve times root three plus one; the height is thirty-two point eight metres.
visuals.caption: Same side: the far distance exceeds the near one by the gap.

visuals.alt: A tower FT seen by a walker, first from A at an angle of elevation of 36 degrees and then from B, 24 metres closer on the same straight path to the foot F, at 52 degrees.
visuals.caption: A walker moves $24$ m towards the tower: the elevation rises from $36^\circ$ to $52^\circ$.

visuals.alt: Working table for the walker: the distances from the foot are h cotangent thirty-six degrees and h cotangent fifty-two degrees; they differ by twenty-four, so h times zero point five nine five one equals twenty-four, giving a height of forty point three metres; the second point is thirty-one point five metres from the foot.
visuals.caption: Cotangent turns each angle into a distance from the foot.

sections.heading: 6. Opposite sides and an object on top
sections.body_md:
**Opposite sides.** From a height $h$ the angles of depression to two points on opposite sides of the foot are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. By alternate angles the distances from the foot are $h\cot\alpha$ and $h\cot\beta$, and they **add**:

$$AB = h\cot\alpha + h\cot\beta.$$

**An object on top.** From a point $x$ from the foot, the bottom and the top of the object are seen at $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Its length is $x\tan\beta - x\tan\alpha$.

*Example:* $48$ m, depressions $60^\circ$ and $45^\circ$: $AB = 16\sqrt{3} + 48 = 75.7$ m.

key_terms.definition_md: Equal angles between parallel lines on opposite sides of a transversal.

formulas.label: Length of an object on top

visual.alt: A sky-walk D, 48 metres above the point F on level ground, with two points A and B on opposite sides of F. From D the angle of depression of A on the left is 60 degrees and of B on the right is 45 degrees. Dashed horizontal lines through D show where the angles are measured from.
visual.caption: Opposite sides: the two distances add, $AB = AF + FB$.

rows: at $A$ the elevation is $60^\circ$; at $B$ it is $45^\circ$

visuals.alt: Working table: by alternate angles the elevations at the two points are sixty and forty-five degrees; the left point is forty-eight cotangent sixty degrees, which is sixteen root three, from the foot; the right point is forty-eight metres away; on opposite sides the distances add, giving seventy-five point seven metres.
visuals.caption: Opposite sides: add the two distances.

visuals.alt: A temple tower with a finial BT on top. From a point P on level ground 36 metres from the foot F of the tower, the angle of elevation of the bottom B of the finial is 45 degrees and of its top T is 52 degrees. The finial length f is the difference of the two heights.
visuals.caption: Finial $f = FT - FB$, with both heights read from the same base $PF$.

visuals.alt: Working table for the finial: the bottom is thirty-six metres high since tangent forty-five degrees is one; the top is thirty-six times one point two seven nine nine, which is forty-six point zero eight metres; the finial is the difference, ten point one metres.
visuals.caption: Subtract two heights read from the same base.

visuals.alt: An 18 metre building AG and a tower FT on the same level ground. From the top A of the building, the foot F of the tower is seen at an angle of depression of 60 degrees and the top T at an angle of elevation of 30 degrees. The dashed line AX is horizontal.
visuals.caption: Depression $60^\circ$ to the foot, elevation $30^\circ$ to the top: two triangles at $A$.

visuals.alt: Working table for the building and tower: the foot of the tower is eighteen cotangent sixty degrees, which is six root three metres from the building; the part of the tower above the roof is six root three times tangent thirty degrees, which is six metres; so the tower is eighteen plus six, twenty-four metres.
visuals.caption: The ground distance is common to the lower and upper triangles.

sections.heading: 7. Checklist and scope
sections.body_md:
1. Draw a labelled figure; mark the horizontal and the angle.
2. Find the shared side (height or distance).
3. Same side: subtract the distances. Opposite sides: add them.
4. Include the eye height if the observer is not at ground level.
5. Check the answer is sensible; give units and the stated precision.

Doubling the distance does not halve the angle: use the ratio.

*Not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus:* problems involving more than two right-angled triangles, and three-dimensional problems. Every problem in this chapter uses at most two right-angled triangles in one vertical plane.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance between two observation points, equal to the difference (same side) or the sum (opposite sides) of their distances from the foot.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *One-triangle problem (2–3 marks):* figure or angle identified 1; ratio equation 1; answer with units 1.
- *Two-triangle problem (3–4 marks):* figure 1; first triangle 1; second triangle or linking equation 1; answer 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Measuring an angle of depression from the vertical.
2. Multiplying where the height must be divided (unknown distance).
3. Forgetting the eye height.
4. Treating the walked distance as the distance to the foot.
5. Adding distances for points on the same side (or subtracting for opposite sides).
6. Rounding in the middle of the working, or not stating the precision.

cards.front_md: What is the **angle of elevation**?
cards.back_md: The angle above the horizontal through the eye, up to the line of sight to an object above eye level.

cards.front_md: What is the **angle of depression**?
cards.back_md: The angle below the horizontal through the eye, down to the line of sight to an object below eye level.

cards.front_md: From which line are both angles measured?
cards.back_md: The horizontal through the observer's eye, never the vertical.

cards.front_md: Why does the depression at the top equal the elevation at the bottom?
cards.back_md: The horizontal through the top is parallel to the ground, so the two angles are alternate angles.

cards.front_md: Value of $\tan 30^\circ$?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

cards.front_md: Value of $\tan 45^\circ$?
cards.back_md: $1$, so at $45^\circ$ the distance equals the height.

cards.front_md: Value of $\tan 60^\circ$?
cards.back_md: $\sqrt{3}$

cards.front_md: How accurate are table values?
cards.back_md: Rounded to four decimal places, so answers found with them are approximate.

cards.front_md: Which ratio links the height and the ground distance?
cards.back_md: Tangent: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$.

cards.front_md: A rope of length $L$ makes angle $\theta$ with the ground. Height?
cards.back_md: $L\sin\theta$ (the rope is the hypotenuse).

cards.front_md: A rope of length $L$ makes angle $\theta$ with the ground. Horizontal reach?
cards.back_md: $L\cos\theta$

cards.front_md: Known height $h$ and angle $\theta$: ground distance?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{h}{\tan\theta}$

cards.front_md: Known distance $d$ and angle $\theta$: height?
cards.back_md: $d\tan\theta$

cards.front_md: A kite string $80$ m long at $30^\circ$: height?
$48$ m from a tower at $52^\circ$, $\tan 52^\circ = 1.2799$: height?
Observer's eyes are $e$ m high. Height of the object?
cards.back_md: $e + d\tan\theta$: add the eye height at the end.

cards.front_md: When do you round the answer?
cards.back_md: Once, at the end, to the precision asked; keep surds or extra decimals in the working.

cards.front_md: Why is the walked distance not the distance to the foot?
cards.back_md: It is only the gap between two points; two triangles with a shared height are needed.

cards.front_md: Two points on the same side, gap $d$, elevations $\alpha$ (far) and $\beta$ (near): height?
cards.back_md: $h = \dfrac{d}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$

cards.front_md: Same side: do the distances add or subtract?
cards.back_md: Subtract: the far distance exceeds the near one by the gap.

cards.front_md: Opposite sides: do the distances add or subtract?
cards.back_md: Add: they lie on either side of the foot.

cards.front_md: Opposite sides, depressions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from height $h$: distance between the points?
cards.back_md: $h\cot\alpha + h\cot\beta$

cards.front_md: Length of an object on top of a tower, seen at $\alpha$ (bottom) and $\beta$ (top) from distance $x$?
cards.back_md: $x\tan\beta - x\tan\alpha$

cards.front_md: $\cot 30^\circ$ and $\cot 60^\circ$?
cards.back_md: $\sqrt{3}$ and $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

cards.front_md: Does doubling the distance halve the angle of elevation?
cards.back_md: No. A $30$ m tower is seen at $45^\circ$ from $30$ m but only $26.6^\circ$ from $60$ m.

cards.front_md: How many right triangles may a problem use in this syllabus?
cards.back_md: At most two, in one vertical plane. Three-dimensional problems are not included.

cards.front_md: First step in any heights-and-distances problem?
cards.back_md: Draw a labelled figure and mark the horizontal and the angle.

questions.stem_md: A drone pilot stands on an open field and looks up at her drone. The angle of elevation of the drone is the angle between

options.text_md: the line of sight to the drone and the horizontal through her eye
the line of sight to the drone and the vertical through her eye
the horizontal through her eye and the ground she stands on
the line of sight and the ground directly below the drone

questions.solution_md: The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal through the observer's eye to the line of sight. The vertical line, the ground and the point below the drone are not the reference line.

questions.stem_md: A guard on a watchtower looks down at a stray cow in the field. The angle of depression of the cow is measured between the line of sight and

options.text_md: the line joining the cow to the foot of the tower
the horizontal line through the guard's eye
the vertical wall of the watchtower
the ground on which the cow stands

questions.solution_md: The angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal through the observer's eye to the line of sight, so the reference line is the horizontal through the guard's eye.

questions.stem_md: From a point on the ground $45$ m from the foot of a temple gateway, the angle of elevation of the top of the gateway is $30^\circ$. Using exact values, the height of the gateway is
questions.solution_md: The height is opposite the angle and $45$ m is adjacent, so $h = 45\tan 30^\circ = 45 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} = 15\sqrt{3}$ m. Option (d) uses $\tan 60^\circ$, (a) uses $\sin 30^\circ$ and (b) divides by $\sin 30^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A kite string, pulled taut, is $40$ m long and makes $45^\circ$ with the level ground. Ignoring any sag, the height of the kite above the ground is
questions.solution_md: The string is the hypotenuse and the height is opposite the angle, so $h = 40\sin 45^\circ = 40 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = 20\sqrt{2}$ m. Option (a) divides by $\sin 45^\circ$ and (b) is the horizontal reach $40\cos 45^\circ$ halved.

questions.stem_md: A helicopter hovers $80$ m directly above a point on a straight road. A motorist on the road is seen at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. The horizontal distance of the motorist from the point below the helicopter is
questions.solution_md: By alternate angles the angle at the motorist is $30^\circ$, so the distance $d$ is adjacent and $80$ m is opposite: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{80}{d}$, giving $d = 80\cot 30^\circ = 80\sqrt{3}$ m. Option (b) multiplies by $\tan 30^\circ$ instead.

questions.stem_md: A telecom pole is seen from a point $50$ m from its foot at an angle of elevation of $36^\circ$. Using $\tan 36^\circ = 0.7265$, the height of the pole to the nearest $0.1$ m is
questions.solution_md: $h = 50\tan 36^\circ = 50 \times 0.7265 = 36.3$ m. Option (c) divides by $\tan 36^\circ$, (d) uses $\sin 36^\circ$ and (a) divides by $\sin 36^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A taut rope $26$ m long runs from the top of a flagstaff to a peg on level ground and makes $50^\circ$ with the ground. Using $\sin 50^\circ = 0.7660$ and $\cos 50^\circ = 0.6428$, the height of the flagstaff to the nearest $0.1$ m is
questions.solution_md: The rope is the hypotenuse and the height is opposite the angle: $h = 26\sin 50^\circ = 26 \times 0.7660 = 19.9$ m. Option (d) uses $\cos 50^\circ$, (a) divides by $\sin 50^\circ$ and (b) uses $\tan 50^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A student on a footbridge, with eyes $1.4$ m above the bridge deck, sees the top of a chimney $36$ m away at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. The top of the chimney is above the deck by
questions.solution_md: The part of the chimney above eye level is $36\tan 45^\circ = 36$ m. Adding the height of the eyes above the deck, the top is $36 + 1.4 = 37.4$ m above the deck. Option (a) forgets the eye height and (b) subtracts it.

questions.stem_md: Two points on a straight path leading to the foot of a signal mast are $36$ m apart. From them the top of the mast is seen at elevations of $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ (the nearer point gives the larger angle). The height of the mast is
questions.solution_md: With nearer distance $x$: $h = x\tan 45^\circ$ and $h = (x + 36)\tan 30^\circ$, so $x = \dfrac{x + 36}{\sqrt{3}}$, giving $x(\sqrt{3} - 1) = 36$ and $x = 18(\sqrt{3} + 1)$. Then $h = x = 18(\sqrt{3} + 1)$ m. Option (b) is the nearer distance when the angles are swapped.

questions.stem_md: A survey drone hovers $60$ m above a straight canal path. Two markers on the path, one on each side of the point directly below the drone, are seen at angles of depression of $45^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. The distance between the markers is
questions.solution_md: By alternate angles the markers are $60\cot 45^\circ = 60$ m and $60\cot 30^\circ = 60\sqrt{3}$ m from the point below the drone. They lie on opposite sides, so the distance between them is $60 + 60\sqrt{3} = 60(\sqrt{3} + 1)$ m. Option (c) is the distance if both were on one side.

questions.stem_md: The height of a lamp post is to be found from the length of the taut cable that runs from its top to a point on level ground and the angle the cable makes with the ground. The ratio that gives the height directly is
questions.solution_md: The cable is the hypotenuse and the height is the side opposite the angle, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{cable}}$ and $h = \text{cable} \times \sin\theta$. Cosine would give the horizontal reach and tangent needs the horizontal distance.

questions.stem_md: The top of a $7$ m pole is joined by a wire to a point on level ground $24$ m from its foot. The cosine of the angle that the wire makes with the ground is
questions.solution_md: The wire is the hypotenuse: $\sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25$ m. The ground distance is adjacent to the angle, so the cosine is $\dfrac{24}{25}$. Option (a) is the sine, (b) the tangent and (c) the secant.

questions.stem_md: A pylon is $25$ m tall. A point $P$ on level ground is $25\sqrt{3}$ m from the foot of the pylon. The angle of elevation of the top of the pylon from $P$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{25}{25\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, and $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$. Option (b) has the ratio inverted.

questions.stem_md: A hiker walks $40$ m straight towards a watchtower on level ground, and the angle of elevation of its top increases from $25^\circ$ to $38^\circ$. Using $\cot 25^\circ = 2.1445$ and $\cot 38^\circ = 1.2799$, the height of the watchtower to the nearest $0.1$ m is
questions.solution_md: With height $h$: $h\cot 25^\circ - h\cot 38^\circ = 40$, so $h = \dfrac{40}{2.1445 - 1.2799} = \dfrac{40}{0.8646} = 46.3$ m. Option (c) is $40\cot 25^\circ$, (d) is $40\cot 38^\circ$ and (a) is $40(\tan 38^\circ - \tan 25^\circ)$.

questions.stem_md: Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on level ground in line with the foot $F$ of a mast $FT$, with $Q$ between $P$ and $F$ and $PQ = d$. The angles of elevation of $T$ from $P$ and $Q$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, with $\beta > \alpha$. If $QF = x$, which equation is correct?
questions.solution_md: Both triangles share the height $FT$. From $Q$: $FT = x\tan\beta$. From $P$, which is $x + d$ from $F$: $FT = (x + d)\tan\alpha$. Equating the two expressions for $FT$ gives (c).

questions.stem_md: From a point $50$ m from the foot of a temple tower, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of its golden finial are $40^\circ$ and $48^\circ$. Using $\tan 40^\circ = 0.8391$ and $\tan 48^\circ = 1.1106$, the height of the finial to the nearest $0.1$ m is
questions.solution_md: The finial is the difference of the two heights: $50\tan 48^\circ - 50\tan 40^\circ = 50(1.1106 - 0.8391) = 50 \times 0.2715 = 13.6$ m. Option (a) is the height of the top alone, (b) adds the two heights and (c) uses $\tan 8^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: From the top of a $60$ m tower, the angles of depression of the top and the foot of a pole on the same level ground are $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. The height of the pole is
questions.solution_md: The foot is $60\cot 45^\circ = 60$ m away, and this is also the horizontal distance to the top of the pole. The drop from the tower top to the pole top is $60\tan 30^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}$ m, so the pole is $60 - 20\sqrt{3}$ m tall. Option (b) is the drop itself.

questions.stem_md: From the roof of a $24$ m apartment block, the top of a tower on the same level ground is seen at an elevation of $30^\circ$ and its foot at a depression of $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is
questions.solution_md: The tower's foot is $24\cot 60^\circ = 8\sqrt{3}$ m away. The part of the tower above the roof is $8\sqrt{3}\tan 30^\circ = 8$ m, so the tower is $24 + 8 = 32$ m tall. Option (d) subtracts the $8$ m and (c) doubles the block.

questions.stem_md: The top of a pole is seen from a point on level ground at an angle of elevation of $45^\circ$. How does the observer's distance from the foot of the pole compare with the height of the pole?

options.text_md: It is equal to the height.

questions.solution_md: $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so $\dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}} = 1$ and the distance equals the height. The two legs of the right triangle are equal.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist rides straight away from a clock tower along a level road. While she rides, the angle of elevation of the clock face from her eye
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$, and the height is fixed while the distance grows, so $\tan\theta$ and therefore $\theta$ decrease.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The angle of depression of a delivery van seen from a library roof equals the angle of elevation of the library roof seen from the van.

**Reason (R):** The horizontal through the roof and the level ground are parallel lines, and the line of sight is a transversal, so the two angles are alternate angles.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal, and this is exactly why the depression equals the elevation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A taut $10$ m rope inclined at $30^\circ$ to level ground reaches a height of $5$ m.

**Reason (R):** $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: the rope is the hypotenuse, so the height is $10\sin 30^\circ = 5$ m. R is also true as a value, but it does not explain A, which depends on $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$, not on the tangent.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** As a walker comes closer to the foot of a tall tower on level ground, the angle of elevation of its top keeps increasing.

**Reason (R):** The angle of elevation is measured from the vertical line through the observer to the line of sight.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$ grows as the distance shrinks. R is false: the angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal, not from the vertical.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A $30$ m flagpole is seen from a point on level ground $30$ m from its foot. The angle of elevation of its top is $60^\circ$.

**Reason (R):** In a right triangle, the tangent of an acute angle is the opposite side divided by the adjacent side.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true. By R, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{30}{30} = 1$, so $\theta = 45^\circ$, not $60^\circ$. A is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A street lamp seen from a point $20$ m from its foot at an elevation of $45^\circ$ is $20$ m high (the observer's eye is at ground level).

**Reason (R):** $\sin 45^\circ$ and $\cos 45^\circ$ have the same value.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true because $\tan 45^\circ = 1$ gives height $= 20$ m. R is a true fact, but A is explained by $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, not by the equality of sine and cosine, so R is not the explanation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** As a speedboat approaches the foot of a $50$ m sea-wall, the angle of depression of the boat from the top of the wall increases.

**Reason (R):** For a fixed height, the tangent of the angle of depression equals height divided by distance, and this grows as the distance shrinks.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The tangent of an acute angle increases with the angle, so a larger value of $\dfrac{50}{d}$ means a larger angle, which is exactly the explanation given.

questions.stem_md: The line of sight to a boat that is below the level of the observer's eye makes an angle of elevation with the horizontal.
questions.solution_md: False. A line of sight to an object below eye level makes an angle of depression with the horizontal; the angle of elevation is for objects above eye level.

questions.stem_md: If a boat is seen from a cliff top at an angle of depression of $45^\circ$, the boat is as far from the foot of the cliff as the cliff is high.
questions.solution_md: True. $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so $\dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}} = 1$ and the horizontal distance equals the height.

questions.stem_md: A tower's top is seen at $30^\circ$ from a point $P$ and, from a point $Q$ on the same side and in line with $P$, at $60^\circ$. Then $P$ is three times as far from the foot of the tower as $Q$ is.
questions.solution_md: True. The distances are $h\cot 30^\circ = h\sqrt{3}$ and $h\cot 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$, and $\sqrt{3} \div \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A $15$ m pole is seen at an elevation of $30^\circ$ from a point $30$ m from its foot.
questions.solution_md: False. A point $30$ m away at $30^\circ$ sees a pole of height $30\tan 30^\circ = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3$ m, not $15$ m.

questions.stem_md: A table value such as $\tan 52^\circ = 1.2799$ is exact, so a height found with it needs no rounding.
questions.solution_md: False. Table values are rounded to four decimal places, so a height found with them is an approximation and must be rounded to the precision asked.

questions.stem_md: The horizontal line through the observer's eye is the reference line for the angle of elevation and also for the angle of depression.
questions.solution_md: True. Both angles are measured from the horizontal through the eye, upward to an object above eye level for elevation and downward to an object below it for depression.

questions.stem_md: From a point on level ground that is not at the foot of a pillar, the angle of elevation of the pillar's top is always less than $90^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: True. The right triangle has a non-zero base, so its angle at the observer is acute: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$ is finite, which means $\theta < 90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The angle between the horizontal through the eye and the line of sight to an object below eye level is called the angle of ___.
questions.solution_md: An object below eye level is seen at an angle of depression, measured downward from the horizontal.

questions.stem_md: A rope-way cable $100$ m long rises at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$. Its vertical rise is ___ m.
questions.solution_md: Vertical rise $= 100\sin 30^\circ = 100 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 50$ m.

questions.stem_md: A bin in the lane is seen from a window $12$ m above the ground at an angle of depression of $45^\circ$. The bin is ___ m from the wall of the building.
questions.solution_md: $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{12}{d}$ gives $d = 12 \div 1 = 12$ m.

questions.stem_md: A point $P$ on level ground is $35\sqrt{3}$ m from the foot of a $35$ m tower. The angle of elevation of the top from $P$ is ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{35}{35\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\theta = 30$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: A stone on the ground is seen from the top of a $10$ m wall at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. The line of sight from the top of the wall to the stone is ___ m long.
questions.solution_md: $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{10}{L}$, so $L = \dfrac{10}{1/2} = 20$ m.

questions.stem_md: With $\tan 40^\circ = 0.8391$, a tank is seen at an elevation of $40^\circ$ from a point $18$ m from its foot. Its height, correct to one decimal place, is ___ m.
In the trigonometric tables, the value of $\tan 45^\circ$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: A $45^\circ$ right triangle has equal legs, so $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.

questions.stem_md: A surveyor measures the angle of elevation of the top of a radio mast from two points $A$ and $B$, which are $35$ m apart in line with the foot of the mast, as $28^\circ$ at $A$ and $41^\circ$ at $B$ (with $B$ nearer). Using $\cot 28^\circ = 1.8807$ and $\cot 41^\circ = 1.1504$, find the height of the mast in metres, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: The heights from both triangles are equal: $h\cot 28^\circ - h\cot 41^\circ = 35$. So $h = \dfrac{35}{1.8807 - 1.1504} = \dfrac{35}{0.7303} = 47.9$ m.

questions.stem_md: The top of a factory chimney is seen from a point $65$ m from its base at an angle of elevation of $38^\circ$. Using $\tan 38^\circ = 0.7813$, find the height of the chimney in metres, correct to one decimal place.

A cable-car station on a ridge is $120$ m above the level of a lake. A jetty on the lake is seen from the station at an angle of depression of $20^\circ$. Using $\tan 20^\circ = 0.3640$, find the horizontal distance from the station to the jetty in metres, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: The angle of elevation of the station from the jetty is also $20^\circ$, so $\tan 20^\circ = \dfrac{120}{d}$ and $d = \dfrac{120}{0.3640} = 329.7$ m.

questions.stem_md: A pylon is $45$ m tall and a point on level ground is $60$ m from its foot. Using $\tan 36^\circ = 0.7265$, $\tan 37^\circ = 0.7536$ and $\tan 38^\circ = 0.7813$, find the angle of elevation of the top of the pylon from the point, to the nearest degree.
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{45}{60} = 0.75$. The tables give $\tan 37^\circ = 0.7536$, the closest value to $0.75$, so $\theta = 37$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: A girl whose eyes are $1.6$ m above the ground stands $45$ m from a water tank and sees its top at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$. Taking $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, find the height of the tank in metres, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: The height above her eyes is $45\tan 30^\circ = 15\sqrt{3} = 25.98$ m. Adding her eye height, $h = 25.98 + 1.6 = 27.6$ m.

questions.stem_md: A film drone hovers $80$ m above level ground. Two markers on the ground, on the same side of the point below it and in line with it, are seen at angles of depression of $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. Taking $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, find the distance between the markers in metres, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: The markers are $80\cot 45^\circ = 80$ m and $80\cot 30^\circ = 80\sqrt{3} = 138.56$ m from the point below. On the same side, the distance between them is $138.56 - 80 = 58.6$ m.

questions.stem_md: A student on the roof of a $36$ m building sees a parked cycle at an angle of depression of $40^\circ$. (a) Name the angle in the right triangle at the cycle that is equal to $40^\circ$ and give the reason. (b) Using $\tan 40^\circ = 0.8391$, find how far the cycle is from the foot of the building, to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The angle of elevation of the roof from the cycle is $40^\circ$, because the horizontal through the roof is parallel to the ground and the two angles are alternate angles.

(b) $\tan 40^\circ = \dfrac{36}{d}$, so $d = \dfrac{36}{0.8391} = 42.9$ m.

questions.solution_md: Use alternate angles, then tan of the angle at the cycle with the height opposite.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Elevation of the roof, alternate angles

questions.stem_md: A stay wire holds up a mobile-phone mast. It is fixed at a point $18$ m up the mast and to a hook on level ground, and makes an angle of $50^\circ$ with the ground. Using $\sin 50^\circ = 0.7660$, find the length of the wire correct to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
The $18$ m is opposite the $50^\circ$ angle and the wire is the hypotenuse, so $\sin 50^\circ = \dfrac{18}{L}$.

$L = \dfrac{18}{0.7660} = 23.5$ m.

questions.solution_md: Opposite and hypotenuse: use sine.

questions.stem_md: Karan sees the top of a pillar at an angle of elevation of $35^\circ$ from a point $45$ m from its foot and writes: height $= \dfrac{45}{\tan 35^\circ} = 64.3$ m. Explain his mistake and find the correct height to one decimal place, using $\tan 35^\circ = 0.7002$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Karan divided by $\tan 35^\circ$, but the height is opposite the angle and $45$ m is adjacent, so $\tan 35^\circ = \dfrac{\text{height}}{45}$ and the height must be multiplied by, not divided by, $\tan 35^\circ$.

Correct height $= 45 \times 0.7002 = 31.5$ m.

questions.solution_md: The height is opposite, so multiply the adjacent distance by tan.

marking_scheme.step: Mistake: divided instead of multiplied (height is opposite)

questions.stem_md: A tow rope of length $50$ m runs up a grassy hillside from a post at the bottom to a post at the top and makes an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$ with the level ground at the bottom. Taking $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, find the vertical height of the top post above the bottom post and the horizontal distance between them.

answer.model_answer_md:
Height $= 50\sin 60^\circ = 50 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 25\sqrt{3} = 43.3$ m.

Horizontal distance $= 50\cos 60^\circ = 50 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 25$ m.

questions.solution_md: The rope is the hypotenuse: sine gives the height and cosine gives the horizontal distance.

questions.stem_md: A statue stands on a pedestal. From a point on level ground $60$ m from the base of the pedestal, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of the statue are $35^\circ$ and $42^\circ$. Using $\tan 35^\circ = 0.7002$ and $\tan 42^\circ = 0.9004$, find the height of the statue to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
Height of the bottom of the statue (the pedestal) $= 60\tan 35^\circ = 60 \times 0.7002 = 42.012$ m.

Height of the top $= 60\tan 42^\circ = 60 \times 0.9004 = 54.024$ m.

Height of the statue $= 54.024 - 42.012 = 12.0$ m.

questions.solution_md: Two right triangles share the base of 60 m; subtract the two heights.

questions.stem_md: A viewing tower is $36$ m tall. Two kiosks on the level ground are on opposite sides of the tower and in line with its foot, and are seen from the top at angles of depression of $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ (see the figure). Taking $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, find the distance between the kiosks to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
By alternate angles, the kiosk seen at $60^\circ$ is $36\cot 60^\circ = 36 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 12\sqrt{3}$ m from the foot.

The kiosk seen at $30^\circ$ is $36\cot 30^\circ = 36\sqrt{3}$ m from the foot.

They are on opposite sides, so the distance is $12\sqrt{3} + 36\sqrt{3} = 48\sqrt{3} = 83.1$ m.

questions.solution_md: Find each kiosk's distance from the foot and add them, because they are on opposite sides.

questions.stem_md: A glider flies in a straight line at a constant height of $120$ m. A watcher on the ground sees it at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$, and later, when it is nearer on the same side, at $60^\circ$. Taking $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, find the horizontal distance that the glider covered between the two sightings, to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
Horizontal distance at $30^\circ$: $120\cot 30^\circ = 120\sqrt{3}$ m.

Horizontal distance at $60^\circ$: $120\cot 60^\circ = \dfrac{120}{\sqrt{3}} = 40\sqrt{3}$ m.

Distance covered $= 120\sqrt{3} - 40\sqrt{3} = 80\sqrt{3} = 138.6$ m.

questions.solution_md: The height is common; subtract the two horizontal distances.

questions.stem_md: From a point $A$ on level ground the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is $45^\circ$. Walking $24$ m straight towards the tower to a point $B$, Rhea measures $60^\circ$ and then writes: height $= 24\tan 60^\circ = 41.6$ m. Explain her mistake and find the correct height, taking $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$, to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
Rhea treated $B$ as the foot of the tower. The $24$ m is only the distance $AB$, not the distance from $B$ to the foot, so one right triangle is not enough.

Let $BF = x$. Then $h = x\tan 60^\circ = x\sqrt{3}$ and $h = (x + 24)\tan 45^\circ = x + 24$, so $x(\sqrt{3} - 1) = 24$ and $x = 12(\sqrt{3} + 1)$.

$h = x\sqrt{3} = 12(3 + \sqrt{3}) = 36 + 12\sqrt{3} = 56.8$ m.

questions.solution_md: Both triangles share the height: equate x tan 60° and (x + 24) tan 45°.

marking_scheme.step: Mistake: 24 m is not the distance to the foot

questions.stem_md: A cricketer fielding on the boundary has eyes $1.7$ m above the ground and stands $60$ m from the foot of a floodlight tower. He sees the top at an angle of elevation of $35^\circ$. Using $\tan 35^\circ = 0.7002$, find the height of the tower to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
Height of the top above his eyes $= 60\tan 35^\circ = 60 \times 0.7002 = 42.012$ m.

The tower also includes the height of his eyes above the ground, $1.7$ m.

Height of the tower $= 42.012 + 1.7 = 43.7$ m.

questions.solution_md: The angle is measured at eye level, so add the eye height to 60 tan 35°.

questions.stem_md: A forest officer walks along a straight track towards a fire-watch tower on level ground. At a point $A$ the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $35^\circ$; after walking $28$ m to a point $B$ it is $50^\circ$. Using $\cot 35^\circ = 1.4281$ and $\cot 50^\circ = 0.8391$, find (a) the height of the tower and (b) the distance of $B$ from the foot of the tower, each correct to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the height be $h$ and let $F$ be the foot. Then $AF = h\cot 35^\circ$ and $BF = h\cot 50^\circ$, and $AF - BF = 28$.

$h(1.4281 - 0.8391) = 28$, so $0.5890\,h = 28$.

(a) $h = \dfrac{28}{0.5890} = 47.5$ m.

(b) $BF = h\cot 50^\circ = 47.5 \times 0.8391 = 39.9$ m.

questions.solution_md: Subtract the two horizontal distances to get 28 m, solve for h, then find BF.

marking_scheme.step: AF = h cot 35° and BF = h cot 50°

questions.stem_md: The figure shows a $15$ m building $AG$ and a tower $FT$ on the same level ground. From the top $A$ of the building, the foot $F$ of the tower is seen at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$ and the top $T$ at an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.

answer.model_answer_md:
The horizontal $AX$ is parallel to $GF$, so $\angle AFG = 30^\circ$ (alternate angles), and $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{15}{GF}$ gives $GF = 15\sqrt{3}$ m.

In the upper triangle, $AX = GF = 15\sqrt{3}$ m and $\angle TAX = 60^\circ$.

$TX = 15\sqrt{3}\tan 60^\circ = 15\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 45$ m.

The tower is $FT = FX + XT = 15 + 45 = 60$ m tall.

questions.solution_md: The distance from the building to the tower is common to both triangles.
